## The idea

Remove every short note between a melody's long arrivals and a plain harmonic
skeleton appears. Put the short notes back and the line acquires momentum. The
extra pitches may fall outside the current chord, but they are organised by
where they come from and where they go.

A *passing tone* fills the step between two chord tones. A *neighbour tone*
leaves a chord tone by step and returns. A *suspension* holds a previous chord
tone into the next harmony before resolving downward. An *anticipation* arrives
early on a tone belonging to the next chord. These are behaviours over time,
not labels attached to isolated pitch classes.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 88
use_synth :piano

define :play_phrase do |events|
  events.each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.82
    sleep duration
  end
end

skeleton = [[:c4, 2], [:e4, 2], [:g4, 2], [:c5, 2]]

passing = [[:c4, 1], [:d4, 1], [:e4, 2],
           [:g4, 1], [:a4, 1], [:c5, 2]]

neighbor = [[:c4, 1], [:d4, 0.5], [:c4, 0.5], [:e4, 2],
            [:g4, 1], [:f4, 0.5], [:g4, 0.5], [:c5, 2]]

decorated = [[:c4, 1], [:d4, 1], [:e4, 1], [:f4, 1],
             [:g4, 1], [:a4, 0.5], [:b4, 0.5], [:c5, 2]]

[skeleton, passing, neighbor, decorated].each do |events|
  play_phrase events
  sleep 1
end
```

The skeleton exposes four stable targets and little else. Passing notes connect
targets by step. Neighbours create local motion around one target. The decorated
version increases density toward the final C, so the same harmonic outline gains
direction.

## Change one thing

1. Change D in the passing version to D-sharp. It still lies between C and E in
   register, but the unequal steps give the connection another colour.
2. Hold F across a change from an F-major accompaniment to C major, then resolve
   it to E. Hear the suspension as prepared tension followed by a downward step.
3. Move the final C half a beat early while the previous harmony continues.
   That pitch becomes an anticipation only because the next chord makes C stable.

## Why it works

Chord membership is evaluated against time. C can be a chord tone over C major,
a decoration over D minor, or an anticipation before A minor. A melody event
therefore needs an aligned harmony event before the category can be computed.

Reduction selects structurally stable notes, often those on strong beats or with
long durations. Decoration then explains the paths between them. The process is
lossy and interpretive. Two analysts can choose different skeletons when rhythm
or harmony is ambiguous. Playing both versions makes the disagreement concrete.

The arrays keep pitch and duration paired. A classifier could add `:role` to an
event, but the renderer would still consume the original note and timing. That
annotation belongs to analysis data rather than playback logic.

Metric position influences the reading. A dissonant passing tone on a weak
half-beat can disappear into motion. Hold the same pitch across a strong beat and
it demands an explanation, perhaps as a suspension. Duration has a similar
effect. The classification arises from pitch, harmony, onset, and destination
together. A set-membership check can identify non-chord tones, but it cannot name
their behaviour without neighbouring events.

Reduction is also a compositional tool. Start from the skeleton and ask what each
gap needs: directness, delay, or a small detour. Add one decoration and replay the
line. When every gap receives a flourish, the stable notes lose their hierarchy.
The alternating versions in the program keep that trade-off audible.

## Take it further

Write a two-bar melody over C major then G major. Include and label one passing
tone, one neighbour, one suspension, and one anticipation. Store each event as a
hash with `:note`, `:start`, `:duration`, and `:role`. Write a renderer that
ignores `:role`, then print a second reduction containing only events labelled
`:chord_tone`.
